en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks requested much thread during the robe-making season.
Even when the robe was finished, much thread remained.
Then it occurred to the group-of-six monks:
“Come, friends, let us request more thread and have the weavers weave us a robe.
Then the group-of-six monks requested more thread and had the weavers weave them a robe.
Even when the robe was woven, much thread remained over.
A second time, the group-of-six monks, having requested more thread, had robe-cloth woven by weavers.
When the robe was finished, much thread remained over.
A third time, the group-of-six monks, having requested yet more thread, had robe-cloth woven by weavers.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying,
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, having themselves requested thread, have weavers weave a robe for them?
The monks heard those people criticizing, grumbling, and complaining.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks, having themselves requested thread, have weavers weave a robe for them?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monks, that you yourselves requested thread and had robes woven by weavers?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you have a thread requested by yourselves and then have robe-cloth woven by weavers?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘If a monk has a robe-cloth woven by weavers after having himself requested the thread, that is an offense of expiation.’"
“Whatever monk, having personally requested thread, should have a robe woven by weavers, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
“Whatever monk” means whichever such person... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Sāma" means:
Having requested it oneself.
"Sutta" refers to six types of suttas: [the *samyutta*, *kevala*, *veyyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, and *itivuttaka*].
"Linens, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, or jute.
"By weavers" means he has them woven by spinners; for each instance of the action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By the mere acquisition [of it], it becomes subject to relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was caused to be woven by weavers after I myself requested the thread, is to be forfeited.
I now forfeit it to the Saṅgha. …pe…
"She should give" ... [and so on] ... "they should give" ... [and so on] ... "I give to the Venerable One."
If it has been caused to be woven and he perceives that it has been caused to be woven, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has been caused to be woven and he is uncertain about it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has been caused to be woven and he perceives that it has not been caused to be woven, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If [the robe] has not been caused to be woven, but one perceives that it has been caused to be woven, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the robe] has not been caused to be woven, but one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the robe] has not been caused to be woven, and one perceives that it has not been caused to be woven, there is no offense.
There is no offense in sewing a robe or in a waistband.
A waistband,
a shoulder strap,
and a bowl bag.
In a water-strainer,
among relatives,
or when invited.
For the sake of another,
with one's own wealth,
[or] for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The sixth training rule on verbal intimation in the Sutta [Vibhaṅga] is finished.
